2.9   Despite any other provision of these rules, the Court may
order any practice and procedure it considers appropriate for a class
proceeding under the Class Proceedings Act to achieve the objects
of that Act.

BOOK_A.title: Class Proceedings Practice and Procedure
BOOK_A.commentary:
A. Generally
The Class Proceedings Act (2003)⁹
makes signiﬁcant changes to this topic.¹⁰
Before it came
into force, some courts followed some of the Institute’s recommendations later embodied there,¹¹
such as prior certiﬁcation. Curiously, this topic is also covered elsewhere in the Rules, in R.13.11,
so much of the commentary on class actions is in the notes to R.13.11.

A great many cases outside Alberta have certiﬁed class actions, and a number of Alberta
cases do so also.¹
Evidence may not be as important in these certiﬁcation applications as it is in other applications
in the Court of King’s Bench. The strength of the cause of action is not really reviewed at this
stage, and the justice bases his or her conclusion on the statement of claim, not on evidence. And
most of the other statutory tests (described in Parts B to F below) are not factual topics amenable
to conventional proof by evidence and involve legal conclusions and the justice’s experience and
the submissions.²
B. The Test
Under this procedure, a few people can nominate themselves as plaintiffs and sue on behalf
of a class. Notice to all is necessary, and all will be bound.³
But other members of the class need
neither consent, nor nominate the named plaintiffs who sue. The tension (conﬂict) here is between
efﬁciency and fairness. Class actions are often economical and efﬁcient,⁴
share expenses, and
deter potential wrongdoers from breaking duties to the public. Their purpose is to give an efﬁcient
means of recovery where individual suits would be expensive or impractical.⁵
No court leave is required merely to commence a class action,⁶
though one can probably
count on a defendant’s challenging it once started. Usually the plaintiffs move to have the court
certify their action as a valid class action.
There are ﬁve necessary (but not sufﬁcient) criteria for a class action and its certiﬁcation:⁷
1. A cause of action;⁸

2. A class¹
which can be clearly and objectively²
deﬁned in advance.³
Whether individual
issues would predominate goes to preferred procedure (#5 below is not to whether there
is an identiﬁable class.⁴
3. An issue or Issues of fact or law which are common to all members,⁵
i. e. deciding them is
necessary (though maybe not sufﬁcient) to decide each member’s claim. But all members
need not be identically situate vis-à-vis the defendant,⁶
nor need there always be more
common issues than separate issues, though that balance is relevant.⁷
A substantial

ingredient common to all is necessary, but there can be sub-classes;¹
if one member
succeeds, that must mean that all will, though maybe to different extents;²
there can be
no conﬂicting interests inside the class.³
There should be a rational connection between
the proposed class deﬁnition and the proposed common issues;⁴
4. The representatives will adequately represent the class;⁵
and ordinarily will belong to it.⁶
See further Part C below.
5. A class action is the preferable procedure,⁷
for the fair and efﬁcient resolution of the
common issues.⁸
Whether a class action is the preferable procedure is assessed in light
of the main goals of class actions: judicial economy, behavior modiﬁcation, and access
to justice.⁹
One compares simplicity and economy of separate lawsuits, against those
for a class action, looking practically.¹⁰
Preferability is assessed in context of the whole
action, and the impact on class members, defendants, and the court.¹¹
The aim is the
best procedure, not perfection.¹²
If the common "issues" are straightforward and many not
disputed, then trying those common issues would not save much duplication.¹³
Often this

test #5 is fairly easy to meet, but not where a multi-province class action is proposed,
especially where the relevant statutes vary province to province.¹
Decisions from other provinces²
are worth looking at, but one must be careful, as most of the
criteria are set by provincial statutes, which vary somewhat province to province.
If you have any doubt about applicability of these rules to your circumstances, you should ask
yourself questions like these ones:
1. Is there a reasonably clear cause of action between the members of the class and the
defendant?³
2. Can membership in the class from the outset be easily and deﬁnitely objectively
ascertained?⁴
3. Are individual determinations of size of awards necessary?
4. Does the cause of action depend on individual circumstances (e. g. , misrepresentation) ?
Or, will success for one mean success for all?
5. Has provision been made for discovery (questioning) or costs?
6. Is there a plan for dealing with or notifying individuals who may be unwilling to be part of
the representative action, or whose claims might be affected (e. g. , by res judicata) ?
7. Will disallowance of the action in representative form give rise to limitation problems for
individual members of the class later on?
The “plain and obvious” test (used to strike out pleadings) need not be satisﬁed to deny a
class action, since denying a class action merely denies one procedure for the suit.⁵
But it is no
bar to certifying a class action, that the defendant has an arguable defence, such as an expired
limitation period.⁶
Where the material shows that a class action would address the interests of all members
of the proposed class, there is no other class action on this matter, and no evidence that other
means would be more practical or efﬁcient, and a class action seems efﬁcient, it may be certiﬁed.⁷
C. The Representative Plaintiff
Relevant criteria for adequacy of proposed named representative plaintiffs are their motive,⁸

absence of conﬂict of interest,¹
competence of their lawyer, and their capacity to pay individual
costs²
(not class costs nor the bill for the suit). They need neither be typical, nor the best possible
representatives, but they must capably and vigorously prosecute. It may require more than one
representative plaintiff.³
If the wronged plaintiffs want different remedies, and face different time limits and interest, a
class suit is not apt, and the court cannot force on the would-be plaintiff a different class than the
class which he or she proposes.
Even if no one is disabled or a minor, a class action needs counsel for the representative
plaintiffs. They cannot self-represent.⁴
The court can replace an unsuitable representative.⁵
Though one plaintiff should not have two similar suits overlapping, a class action not yet
certiﬁed is no bar to an individual suit, especially if a limitation period looms.⁶
Failure to follow up on obvious information needed, or to contact relevant people, were
grounds to hold that the plaintiff would not fairly and adequately represent the interests of the
alleged class.⁷
There was a war between different representative plaintiffs and with a former lawyer for them
who had been removed. The lawyer applied about a year late to appeal approval of a settlement
of the action. The necessary time extension to do so was denied, largely because of the prejudice
which the year’s delay would create. Huge sums had been paid out relying on the settlement,
and the deadline for ﬁling individual claims had passed. The prejudice would be irreparable. The
basis for the class action legislation is letting a few representatives sue and prosecute or settle
an action, albeit under court supervision. If only the active members of the group are bound by a
settlement, the scheme cannot work.⁸
Usually the proposed plaintiff provides a litigation plan; the court evaluates it for adequacy,
but it need not be incapable of improvement.⁹
The court may certify a class action, but specify
necessary improvements if the suit is to go further.¹⁰

The Class Proceedings Act s.13(2) lets the Court substitute a representative plaintiff, but here
the issue was not changing the representative but changing his or her counsel. Such a change
by the court, not by the representative's counsel, involves motives for the choice of counsel, and
any prejudice to the class.¹
Here the same lawyer would continue, but he had changed law ﬁrms.
The test is not which law ﬁrm is better.²
Lawyers have no independent status in a class (or other)
action.³
If the named representative plaintiff includes in the class action an individual claim or two
which is not a common issue, that can slow down the class part of the suit and give that plaintiff's
lawyer a conﬂict of interest. As early negotiations to settle class actions are common, that conﬂict
of interest can have effects very early. The court may temporarily stay the individual claim, and
also make the named plaintiff elect which claim (class or individual) he or she will retain this law
ﬁrm for, to remove the conﬂict of interest.⁴
D. The Class and Subclasses⁵
A class action can be certiﬁed without ﬁnding or being able to ﬁnd the number of class
members; it is enough to ﬁnd that there are others in it besides the named plaintiff.⁶
Others need
not have complained, so long as there is some basis in fact for a common issue.⁷
The deﬁnition
is to be objective, but it has to have some rational relationship with the common issues, and each
class member must have at least a “colorable claim” against the defendant.⁸
Some evidence of
the connection is necessary?⁹
The geographical area in one case was large, yet the cause (a
ruptured pipeline) was known; this was not some vague pollution claim over decades. The larger
the area, the less likely is the class deﬁnition. The defendant admitted that people abutting on
or directly adjacent to the one river and its distributaries downstream would be proper class
members, but no member of that class had ever come forward.¹⁰
While class size alone is not a reason to deny certiﬁcation, a large size makes it far more
likely that the class is over-inclusive and contains members who have no tenable claim against
the defendant.¹¹
In another case, there was such basis for there being people with defective tires outside the
small groups given relief by the defendant in its recall notices.¹²
The proposed class need not be
narrowed at this stage.¹³
The proposed common issues should not be fundamentally changed at
the certiﬁcation stage, but could be adjusted later after certiﬁcation.¹⁴

Where most of the group have joined and funded the suit, the court may decide to include only
those others who elect (after notice) to join.¹
All potential class members should get notice of an
application, and some can opt out.²
Plaintiffs cannot be forced to seek certiﬁcation of their suits as class actions, if the individual
plaintiffs have causes of action.³
If there are subclasses, speciﬁc procedures may be necessary.⁴
That some of those injured by a common wrong might later have settled or waived their rights,
without evidence, is premature speculation and no bar to certiﬁcation.⁵
E. Common Issues and Examples⁶
Non-common issues may have to be decided in individual proceedings, and need for actual
past reliance of individual plaintiffs does not bar a class action.
A class action was not proper in a nuisance suit, because the common issues were a small
fraction of the issues. And resolving them would not speed up resolving the others.⁷
Common
issues predominated, even though different damages and a charging standard of care, and sub-
classes could be needed, in a class action over a residential school.⁸
A proposed class action
against a government regulator was not allowed because the legislation did not create proximity,
and so no reasonable cause of action was disclosed.⁹
No class action against an investment ﬁrm by its clients for negligent investment advice was
preferable, as only a very few of the class had at all similar circumstances, and the number of
questions to be decided for each individual class member would be overwhelming.¹⁰
It is unsuitable
to have a class which needs narrowing, if narrowing would arbitrarily exclude people with an
interest in the common issue.¹¹
A class action was not certiﬁed because the plaintiff did not show anyone else with a similar
claim, and the record made it peculiar to the plaintiff. So a class action was not the preferable
procedure.¹²

The threshold for establishing a common issue in a proposed class proceeding is minimal, but
it still requires each member of the proposed class to possess the same interest and be subject
to the same positive or negative outcome without the need for personalized investigation. If the
action raises issues requiring individual investigation, it will not meet the commonality requirement.
Allegations of deprivations not experienced by the entire proposed class cannot be summated to
prove a common deprivation, as personalized investigation would still be required for a resolution.
Charter claims will generally not meet the commonality requirement of a class proceeding as they
are presumably individual in nature and would require personalized investigation.¹
Things may not be so clear in some circumstances. Most people imagine a class action as
consisting of injured consumers suing a corporate giant in a products case. For little or no upfront
contribution, they can collectively ﬁght battles beyond their individual means. And they can ﬁght
claims which individually would be small and so wholly uneconomical to litigate. However, the
nature of the remedy (e. g. , damages) or the nature of the cause of action (e. g. , misrepresentation)
may in fact make some such claims difﬁcult to mount.²
Section 30(1) of the Class Proceedings Act gives conditions for certifying aggregate damages
as a common issue. It was not alleged the conditions were satisﬁed, only that the defendant had
the records, and the ordinary remedies for breach of contract would sufﬁce.³
F. Suitable Alternative Procedure
Preferable method refers both to substantive relief and to procedure.⁴
Class actions should not be approached restrictively.⁵
The Class Proceedings Act, s.5(2) sets out some criteria for determining the “preferable
procedure”. In other words, better than other methods like joining or consolidating individual
claims.⁶
There are sometimes better procedures, such as trying one test case.⁷
The criteria for the
purposive application of the preferable-procedure test are discussed.⁸
This means preferable, not
just to a group of individual suits, but also preferable to alternatives, including joinder, test cases,
and consolidation.⁹
Efﬁciency and fairness must be balanced in the decision.¹⁰
And “preferable”

involves balancing the interests of all parties and the court, and can involve the resources of
individual class members, economics, number of issues, complexities, and alternative means.¹
Evidence of an identiﬁable class and common issues, is some evidence of a preferable
procedure, if there is no contrary evidence. The same is true if only one person volunteers to
be the plaintiff.²
Also evidence of a preferable procedure is the defendant's intransigence or
intimidation.³
Also evidence of preferable procedure is predominating common issues whose
decision will signiﬁcantly advance the lawsuit.⁴
Also relevant is that the class action is complex
because of the number of different causes of action to be certiﬁed.⁵
Even if the plaintiffs satisfy all criteria, other factors may weigh in the court’s discretion against
a class suit: different defences against different plaintiffs, need for separate examinations for
discovery (questioning), important non-common issues, or a small class (so each member should
be a plaintiff), and need for actual reliance of individual plaintiffs. But irrelevant and no bar to a
class suit, are some need for individual assessment of damages, different contracts, different
remedies, or subgroups with separate issues.⁶
If the plaintiffs moved far too slowly to seek certiﬁcation, but no serious prejudice was caused
by the delay and there was an arguable excuse, the delay need not bar the suit.⁷
Where a regulatory tribunal decided some issues for investors, but not all, and permitted
further suit, and some issues remained, and individual claims were small, a class action was
proper.⁸
What procedure is preferable is largely a question of law, so afﬁdavits and cross-examination
are not necessary.⁹
G. Other Procedural Issues
See also R.2.7 and notes.
Class action legislation is presumed not to allow a superior court to hear a suit which would
otherwise come within the jurisdiction of another court or tribunal, because of its subject matter.¹⁰

The ambiguities and gaps in R.2.6 can be ﬁxed by the courts’ inherent power to settle
procedure.¹
The style of cause of a class action is set by R.13.11 and Form 10.
The usual order for afﬁdavits from and cross-examination of the party moving, before evidence
from the party opposing, was adopted for a certiﬁcation motion, but based on the circumstances of
that one case, with no ﬁrm rule, considering fairness, practicalities, and shortening the process.²
No formal notice is necessary for a suit to be “a proceeding that is the subject of an application
for certiﬁcation”; it is enough that the plaintiffs make that intent plain; then a court order is
necessary for it to revert to an ordinary lawsuit.³
An Alberta class action was started about 7 weeks after a similar Ontario action but before
second and third Ontario class actions. Alberta would not stay its suit, which was further advanced.⁴
Deliberately not ﬁling a statement of defence admits liability to the plaintiff, but the admission
is only by that one defendant, not other defendants, and on a motion to certify a class action does
not show liability, though a criminal prosecutions preliminary transcript may show arguable liability
to the class, as "some basis in fact", as hearsay is admissible.⁵
A justice acting under a settlement of a class suit, approved by a court order, and so giving
distribution directions, acts as a superior court justice and appeals to the Court of Appeal live from
that justice.⁶
A court of appeal owes considerable deference to a chambers decision on whether to certify
a class action.⁷
If a case management judge strikes the representative (class) parts of a statement of claim,
but years later the Court of Appeal ﬁnds error and sends it back to rehear, the case management
judge may well be better suited than it to decide on the merits.⁸
A plaintiff with an individual lawsuit has a right to that suit and can opt out of an overlapping
class action. The court may temporarily stay the individual lawsuit even if its plaintiff opted out of
the class action. The criteria for a stay includes separation or not of issues, resources consumed,
and chance of inconsistent results, and degree of overlap.⁹
Consent (and a proposed settlement) help an application to certify a class action, but are not
sufﬁcient, and the court must still do the usual analysis and consider each criterion to see if it is
satisﬁed.¹⁰

The trial judge has the ultimate authority to add an aggregate damages question even
where this very question was rejected at certiﬁcation. The failure to propose or certify aggregate
damages, or another remedy, as a common issue does not preclude a trial judge from invoking
the provisions if considered appropriate once liability is found.¹
H. Costs
Decisions on costs from other provinces can mislead, as some provinces' legislation bars or
narrowly restricts costs.²
Only Alberta’s class actions legislation requires advance approval of a contingency fee
agreement. Notice should go to the Public Trustee if many involved in the class would not be sui
juris. Notice would ordinarily not be given to the defendant. There are many criteria for approval. A
25% fee is within the range usually negotiated in Alberta for contingency agreements, particularly
as some of the claims would not involve any recovery even if they were completely successful in
law.³
The situation respecting costs of a failed suit, and the legislative and other history of that topic,
are reviewed.⁴
Though some provinces bar costs awards in a class action,⁵
Alberta’s Legislature
has chosen the opposite approach. It was proper for the chambers judge who certiﬁed the action
to refuse to rule in advance on whether costs would be possible, and to leave it until later in the
lawsuit.⁶
Individual members of the group are jointly and severally liable for costs and, arguably, subject
to discovery.⁷
Even in a class action, costs are discretionary and hard to upset on appeal. Class actions
can be very expensive. The plaintiffs and their lawyers here would have reaped huge proﬁts, had
they won. Statutory permission to waive costs against the plaintiffs does not bar making them pay
costs when the Court dismissed the suit on the merits.⁸
Class actions are covered by the general
costs Rules, so success is presumed to bring along costs, and R.10.32 lists extra factors relevant
in a class suit. It is relevant that the suit was over private interests of class members. Here any
uncertainty in the law needed no class action; private suits would do. And behavior modiﬁcation is
irrelevant if there is no illegality. Speculative failed suits should not be spared, even if the plaintiff
was in good faith.⁹
A suit over a failed investment, with no direct public interest (only the notion of
accountability), and no novel point of law, should not be spared costs if it is dismissed.¹⁰

Security for costs is possible in a class action.¹
I. Settlement
In assessing a settlement, the court starts with a concern that class action settlements should
be viewed with suspicion, and investigate all aspects of the proposed settlement and evidence
relevant to the principles to be reviewed. When reviewing an “arm’s length” negotiation, the court
moves to a presumption of fairness. That investigation continues until the court decides whether,
the proposed settlement is “fair, reasonable and in the best interests of the class”.²
When a class action is settled, commonly the court approves both the settlement and the
fees of counsel for the class, often at very large sums.³
Settlements usually ﬁx the fees of the
class' counsel, but if that counsel acts on a number of class actions in different provinces, comity
suggests deferring fee decisions to the court where that counsel is located.⁴
Court approval is
necessary, and depends on whether the settlement is fair, reasonable, and in the best interests
of those affected.⁵
On dissenters challenging a settlement, see Part C above.
A class action's proposed settlement was not approved because it was too broad on what was
released; they might end some other existing class actions. The settlement should release only
the claims certiﬁed (and pleaded) in this present class action.⁶
A multi-jurisdiction class action settled, which had to be approved by courts in a number
of provinces, which led to a lot of applications and appeals. Repeating a point in a number of
provinces is not vexatious, but it does not have to be done. Though the losing parties were not
to be penalized, very large amounts were involved and so costs were set at 3 times column 5 of
Schedule C.⁷

Diffusion Métromédia CMR 2011 SCC 9, [2011] 1 SCR 214.

How important the common issues are in relation to the claims as a whole is one consideration. The test is not convenience or burden of a class action per se, but on the relative advantages of a class action and of other types of litigation: Setoguchi v. Uber 2023 ABCA 45, 52 Alta LR(7th) 264, leave den (SCC 13 Jul ’23), affg 2021 ABQB 18 (¶’s 62-77). This is a high-level macro consideration: Salna v.
